newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - "Saints" seek economic independence for "paradise".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Saints" seek economic independence for "paradise".

text.p: Gourmets in Tokyo say the "Saints" grow a heavenly coffee and Britons in the know say their tuna kebabs are to die for.

But David Smallman, the British governor of the Atlantic Ocean island of St. Helena, says his micro-nation needs more micro-markets to carve its own place in the burgeoning and often brutal global economy.

"We are the size of a very small country town. We have very few natural resources and very few activities which employ labour," he said in an interview aboard the island's small cargo-passenger liner in Cape Town.
St. Helena, best known as Napoleon's place of banishment after his defeat in the Battle of Waterloo, was valued once as a victualling station for ships.

Britain implemented a workfare programme after the collapse of the flax industry on which the island depended more than 30 years ago, setting people to work in the forests, fixing houses and maintaining roads.
"The government employs in the region of 70 to 75 percent of the workforce of 2,000 to 2,400 people...We don't have the resources to meet that expense on our own," Smallman said.
Close to 1,500 islanders work on nearby Ascension Island and in the Falklands. Their remittances of over a million pounds ($1.65 million) a year are the biggest single source of income.
Now London wants the island's 5,500 people to make their own way without the British government's contribution -- 3.4 million pounds this year -- to their budget.
THATCHERITE APPROACH CALLED FOR

"In the most graphic terms, the government of St. Helena is being asked to undertake a structural adjustment to the economy -- to bring to the island Thatcherite concepts -- but in a very much shorter time and without economies of scale," Smallman said.

Already, government forestry projects have been contracted out to island entrepreneurs who do twice as much with a pound and tasks such as the endless mowing of grass that kept men busy at state expense have been reduced.
"We've grasped the very interesting challenge of trying to ensure that government only does what government should do."

After 15 months as the Queen's representative on the island -- a position equivalent to executive president -- Smallman is convinced that the answer lies in attracting new investments to what could be the world's smallest emerging market.
"There's only a small amount of money going round and round on the island. If we can entice private investment from outside then we will be able to create a private economy," he said.
NICHE MARKETS AND TAX BREAKS
One existing 250,000-pound-a-year project produces frozen tuna kebabs popular at British barbeques and the product of the island's tiny 3.5-hectare (8.6-acre) coffee plantation is prized in Tokyo.
Despite a minimum tax holiday of five years, however, the people who call themselves the "Saints" have found few angels to share their corner of paradise.

One deal in place is for a blast-freezing plant to process fish from a new long-liner jointly owned by British and Spanish interests. Fertiliser will partly substitute for some of the island's monthly import aboard the Royal Mail ship St. Helena.

Initially, the project will provide work for 20 to 30 of the 300 registered unemployed, including six deckhands. If it goes well there is talk of a can-making plant that could open up options to can fresh produce as well.
Efforts to persuade a South African clothing maker to set up a finishing plant on the island have failed so far, despite the opportunity to evade European Union restrictions.
"We have no natural resources really other than our labour force, which is relatively well educated, computer literate, speaks English and international in outlook.

"We've got only one very good competitive advantage, which is that as a dependent territory of a member of the European Union we can gain not just tariff-free access to European markets but quota-free access."
HOLIDAYS IN PARADISE
Smallman was in South Africa trying to raise awareness of St. Helena as an exotic tourism destination, but he says this is unlikely ever to be the main source of foreign funds.
The island's ship carries only 128 passengers and visits only 12 times a year from South Africa and from Britain.

"St. Helena is a credible destination. We want to make it a sought-after destination. It's not for the bucket-and-spade brigade -- we have no beaches for a start -- but it has history, excellent walks and tranquility," he said.
The island government, which advises Smallman, has applied for a five-million-pound EU grant to build a breakwater that would allow tourists to land safely from passing cruise liners.
"That won't be the answer, though. Basically, we have to do it on our own and the only way is through inward investment," Smallman said.
($1=1.65 sterling)
